title: Belly Fat: Why Crunches Alone Won't Flatten Your Stomach
subtitle: What actually shrinks the fat around your middle

body.hook: Done 100 sit-ups a day for a month and your waist still hasn't changed? You're not doing it wrong. Your body just doesn't burn fat from the spot you exercise.

sections.heading: What belly fat is
sections.text: There are two kinds of fat around the middle. Subcutaneous fat sits just under the skin, the part you can pinch. Visceral fat lies deeper, around organs like the liver. Visceral fat is the one linked to type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, even in young adults who are not overweight on the scale.

sections.heading: Why it matters at university
sections.text: Long hours sitting in lectures and libraries, late-night short eats, sugary tea and broken sleep all push the body to store fat around the waist. A waist that is more than half your height is an early warning sign worth acting on.

sections.heading: Why spot exercises don't work
sections.text: When you exercise, your body pulls energy from fat stores all over, not only from the muscle you are working. In one study, six weeks of abdominal exercises strengthened the muscles but did not reduce belly fat. Crunches build strong muscles underneath, which is good, but the fat on top only shrinks when overall body fat goes down.

sections.heading: What actually works
sections.text: Belly fat responds well to whole-body changes, and visceral fat is usually the first to go.
bullets: Walk briskly for 30 minutes on most days. Walking between faculties counts.
Swap sugary drinks and sweet tea for water or plain tea with less sugar.
Fill half your plate with vegetables and keep rice to about one fist.
Cut down on fried short eats and kottu late at night.
Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Short sleep raises hunger hormones.

body.key_point: You can't choose where you lose fat, but regular movement, fewer sugary drinks and better sleep shrink belly fat faster than any single exercise.

myths.myth: Crunches burn belly fat.
myths.fact: They strengthen your core but don't target the fat on top. Whole-body activity does.

myths.myth: A flat stomach means you are healthy.
myths.fact: Health depends on many things, including blood pressure, blood sugar, fitness and sleep, not only how your stomach looks.

body.takeaway: Measure your waist, not just your weight. Aim to keep it under half your height.
body.try_this: Tonight, measure your waist at the midpoint between your lowest rib and hip bone. Then take a 15-minute walk after dinner every day this week.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if your waist is growing quickly, or if you also have very high thirst, frequent urination or tiredness, which can be signs of high blood sugar.

references.label: World Health Organization. Obesity and overweight (fact sheet).
Vispute SS et al. The effect of abdominal exercise on abdominal fat. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(9):2559-2564.
Ross R et al. Waist circumference as a vital sign in clinical practice. Nature Reviews Endocrinology. 2020;16:177-189.

title: Too Thin? How to Gain Weight the Healthy Way
subtitle: Building strength without living on junk food

body.hook: Tired of hearing 'eat more!' from everyone back home? Gaining weight can be just as hard as losing it, and doing it with biscuits and fizzy drinks is not the answer.

sections.heading: Why being underweight matters
sections.text: A BMI below 18.5 can mean your body is short of energy, protein, iron and other nutrients. That can show up as tiredness, frequent colds, hair fall, irregular periods and weaker bones later in life.

sections.heading: Common reasons at university
sections.text: Skipping breakfast before early lectures, long gaps between meals, a tight food budget, exam stress that kills your appetite, and very high activity without enough food. Sometimes there is a medical reason, such as an overactive thyroid or a stomach problem.

sections.heading: How to add healthy energy
sections.text: The goal is steady gain of muscle and healthy weight, not belly fat.
bullets: Eat three meals and two or three snacks every day. Do not skip breakfast.
Add an extra cupped hand of rice or a roti to lunch and dinner.
Include protein at every meal: dhal, eggs, fish, chicken, soya or milk.
Snack on peanuts, a banana, curd, milk or a peanut butter sandwich.
Cook with a thumb of oil and add scraped coconut to mallung.
Do strength exercises 2 or 3 times a week so the extra energy builds muscle.

body.key_point: Healthy weight gain comes from more meals, more protein and strength exercise, not from sugary drinks and fried snacks.

myths.myth: Junk food is the fastest way to gain weight.
myths.fact: It adds fat around the middle and little nutrition. Nutrient-rich foods build healthier weight.

body.takeaway: Small, frequent, protein-rich meals plus strength training help you gain weight that makes you stronger.
body.try_this: Pack one extra snack (a banana and a handful of peanuts) in your bag every day this week.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if you are losing weight without trying, have no appetite for weeks, or have frequent diarrhoea, a fast heartbeat or very irregular periods.

references.label: NHS. Advice for underweight adults.
Nutrition Division, Ministry of Health Sri Lanka. Food Based Dietary Guidelines for Sri Lankans. 2021.
World Health Organization. Healthy diet (fact sheet).

title: Stiff Neck From Studying? Fix Your Desk Posture
subtitle: Simple set-up changes for cramped hostel rooms

body.hook: Studying on your bed with the laptop on your knees? Your neck has noticed, even if you haven't.

sections.heading: Why posture matters
sections.text: Looking down at a screen for hours puts extra load on your neck and upper back. Over a semester this can cause neck pain, headaches and tight shoulders. The good news is that small changes to how you sit make a big difference.

sections.heading: Set up your space
sections.text: You don't need special furniture. Use what you have.
bullets: Raise your laptop so the top of the screen is at eye level. A stack of books works.
Sit back in the chair with a rolled towel behind your lower back.
Keep your feet flat on the floor or on a box.
Keep your elbows close to your body at about a right angle.
Sit facing the window side-on, so light doesn't glare on the screen.

sections.heading: Move every 30 minutes
sections.text: The best posture is your next posture. Stand up, roll your shoulders, look at something far away for 20 seconds, and gently turn your head side to side.

body.key_point: Screen at eye level, back supported, and a short movement break every 30 minutes.

myths.myth: Sitting perfectly straight all day prevents pain.
myths.fact: Holding any position too long causes stiffness. Regular movement matters more.

body.takeaway: Raise your screen and move often. Your neck will thank you by exam week.
body.try_this: Set a 30-minute timer when you study today. Each time it rings, stand and do five shoulder rolls.
body.seek_help: See a doctor or physiotherapist if pain lasts more than two weeks, spreads down an arm, or comes with numbness or tingling.

references.label: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). Computer workstations eTool: good working positions.
NHS. Neck pain.

title: PCOS: Knowing the Signs
subtitle: Irregular periods, acne or hair growth? What PCOS is and what helps

body.hook: Periods that come every two or three months, stubborn acne, or new hair on your chin? These can have many causes, and one of the most common is PCOS.

sections.heading: What PCOS is
sections.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition that affects how the ovaries work. It affects about one in ten women of reproductive age. Despite the name, you don't need cysts on your ovaries to have PCOS.

sections.heading: Common signs
sections.text: Signs vary a lot from person to person.
bullets: Irregular, infrequent or very heavy periods
Acne or oily skin
Extra hair on the face, chest or back
Thinning hair on the scalp
Weight gain, especially around the waist
Dark, velvety skin patches on the neck or armpits

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: PCOS is linked to insulin resistance, so it raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol and heart disease later. It can also affect mood and fertility. Early diagnosis and healthy habits lower these risks.

sections.heading: What helps
sections.text: There is no single cure, but PCOS is very manageable.
bullets: Move every day. Activity improves how your body uses insulin.
Choose whole grains like red rice and kurakkan, and plenty of vegetables.
Limit sugary drinks, sweets and refined white flour foods.
Sleep well and manage stress.
Medicines prescribed by a doctor can regulate periods and treat symptoms.

body.key_point: PCOS is common and manageable. Lifestyle changes help every symptom, and a doctor can confirm the diagnosis.

myths.myth: You can't have PCOS if you are slim.
myths.fact: PCOS affects people of all body sizes.

myths.myth: PCOS means you can never have children.
myths.fact: Many people with PCOS conceive, sometimes with medical support.

body.takeaway: Track your periods. A pattern of irregular cycles is worth discussing with a doctor.
body.try_this: Log your next three periods in the cycle tracker so you have a clear record to show a doctor.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if your periods are more than 35 days apart, you have fewer than eight a year, or you notice new hair growth or severe acne. Tracking can't diagnose PCOS; it needs a medical assessment.

references.label: Teede HJ et al. Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2023;108(10):2447-2469.
NHS. Polycystic ovary syndrome.
World Health Organization. Polycystic ovary syndrome (fact sheet).

title: Period Pain: What's Normal and What Helps
subtitle: Getting through cramps on lecture days

body.hook: Missed a practical because the cramps were too much? Period pain is very common, but it shouldn't stop your life every month.

sections.heading: Why periods hurt
sections.text: During a period the womb muscle tightens to shed its lining. Chemicals called prostaglandins cause these contractions, and higher levels mean stronger cramps. Pain usually starts just before or as bleeding begins and eases after 2 or 3 days.

sections.heading: What helps
sections.text: Most period pain can be eased at home.
bullets: Put a hot water bottle or warm cloth on your lower tummy.
Gentle walking, stretching or yoga relaxes the muscles.
Take a pain reliever such as paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed on the pack, if it suits you.
Drink water and eat regular meals; skipping food can make you feel worse.
Rest when you need to and plan lighter study days.

sections.heading: Look after yourself through the cycle
sections.text: Regular exercise, enough sleep and not smoking are linked to less painful periods over time. Keeping a cycle log helps you prepare for heavier days.

body.key_point: Mild to moderate cramps are normal. Pain that stops you studying every month deserves a check-up.

myths.myth: Severe period pain is just something you have to put up with.
myths.fact: Very painful periods can be a sign of conditions like endometriosis, which doctors can treat.

body.takeaway: Heat, gentle movement and simple pain relief help most cramps. Severe pain is not normal.
body.try_this: Next period, try a warm compress and a 10-minute gentle walk, and note in the cycle tracker how you feel.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if pain is severe, lasts longer than usual, you bleed very heavily (soaking a pad every hour), bleed between periods or after sex, or feel faint.

references.label: NHS. Period pain.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Dysmenorrhea: painful periods (FAQ).

title: Why Do I Crave Sweets? The Real Reasons Behind Sugar Cravings
subtitle: And simple ways to manage them without willpower battles

body.hook: It's 4 PM, you're stuck on an assignment, and suddenly you need a chocolate or a sweet bun right now. Sound familiar?

sections.heading: Why cravings happen
sections.text: Cravings are not a lack of willpower. They usually have a reason.
bullets: Long gaps between meals make blood sugar dip, and your brain asks for quick energy.
Short sleep raises the hunger hormone ghrelin and lowers the fullness hormone leptin.
Stress and boredom make sweet food feel comforting.
Habit: if you always have a sweet with tea, your brain expects it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Free sugars in soft drinks, sweet tea, cakes and sweets add energy with no nutrition. Too much raises the risk of weight gain, tooth decay and type 2 diabetes. WHO advises keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy, ideally below 5%, which is about 6 teaspoons.

sections.heading: How to manage cravings
sections.text: Work with your body, not against it.
bullets: Eat regular meals with protein and fibre, such as dhal, eggs, vegetables and red rice.
Keep a better snack ready: a banana, a guava, peanuts or curd.
Drink a glass of water first. Thirst can feel like hunger.
Have a small portion and enjoy it slowly, instead of banning sweets completely.
Reduce the sugar in your tea by one spoon each week.

body.key_point: Cravings usually mean you're hungry, tired or stressed. Fix those and the cravings get weaker.

myths.myth: Jaggery and kithul treacle are healthy sugars.
myths.fact: They have a few minerals but still count as free sugar.

myths.myth: You must cut out sugar completely.
myths.fact: Small amounts as part of a balanced diet are fine. Strict bans often lead to binges.

body.takeaway: Regular meals, enough sleep and a ready healthy snack are your best tools against cravings.
body.try_this: This week, take one spoon less sugar in your tea and keep a fruit in your bag for the afternoon slump.
body.seek_help: If you feel out of control around food, or eat large amounts and then feel guilty, a counsellor or dietitian can help without judgement.

references.label: World Health Organization. Guideline: sugars intake for adults and children. 2015.

Spiegel K et al. Sleep curtailment in healthy young men is associated with decreased leptin levels, elevated ghrelin levels, and increased hunger and appetite. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2004;141(11):846-850.
Malik VS et al. Sugar-sweetened beverages and risk of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis. Diabetes Care. 2010;33(11):2477-2483.

title: Eating Your Feelings? Understanding Emotional Eating
subtitle: When food becomes the answer to stress, boredom or loneliness

body.hook: Ever finished a whole packet of biscuits during a stressful night of revision without really tasting them? That's emotional eating, and almost everyone does it sometimes.

sections.heading: What emotional eating is
sections.text: Emotional eating means eating to cope with feelings rather than hunger. Stress, boredom, loneliness, homesickness and even happiness can all trigger it. The food gives quick comfort, but the feeling usually comes back.

sections.heading: Physical hunger or emotional hunger?
sections.text: A few clues help you tell them apart.
bullets: Physical hunger builds slowly; emotional hunger comes suddenly.
Physical hunger is happy with many foods; emotional hunger wants a specific comfort food.
Physical hunger stops when you're full; emotional eating often continues past full.
Emotional eating is often followed by guilt.

sections.heading: What helps
sections.text: The aim is not to never eat for comfort, but to have more ways to cope.
bullets: Pause for 5 minutes and ask: am I hungry, or am I stressed, bored or tired?
Name the feeling. Writing it down can take away some of its power.
Try a non-food comfort: a walk, a call to a friend, music, a shower.
Eat regular meals so you are not overly hungry when stress hits.
Eat slowly, without your phone, and notice taste and fullness. This is mindful eating.

body.key_point: Emotional eating is normal. Noticing the feeling behind it is the first step to choosing what you really need.

myths.myth: Emotional eating is a sign of weak willpower.
myths.fact: It's a common coping habit, and habits can be changed with support and practice.

body.takeaway: Before you reach for a snack, pause and ask what you are really hungry for.
body.try_this: Next time you want to snack while studying, wait 5 minutes and drink a glass of water. If you're still hungry, eat something you'll enjoy slowly.
body.seek_help: If you often eat very large amounts and feel out of control, or you restrict food and then binge, please talk to a counsellor. Eating disorders are treatable.

references.label: van Strien T. Causes of emotional eating and matched treatment of obesity. Current Diabetes Reports. 2018;18(6):35.

Warren JM, Smith N, Ashwell M. A structured literature review on the role of mindfulness, mindful eating and intuitive eating in changing eating behaviours. Nutrition Research Reviews. 2017;30(2):272-283.

title: Skipping Meals During Exams? Fuel Your Brain Instead
subtitle: Small eating habits that keep focus steady and stop energy crashes

body.hook: Rushing to an 8 AM exam on an empty stomach and a cup of sweet tea? Your brain is running on fumes.

sections.heading: Why skipping meals backfires
sections.text: Your brain uses a steady supply of glucose. Skipping breakfast or lunch can leave you tired, irritable and less able to concentrate. Then hunger hits later and it's easier to overeat short eats or sweets.

sections.heading: Breakfast and learning
sections.text: Studies in young people show that eating breakfast, especially one with slower-release carbohydrates, supports attention and memory through the morning compared with skipping it.

sections.heading: Easy exam-week eating
sections.text: Plan simple, steady meals.
bullets: Breakfast: string hoppers with dhal, an egg and bread, oats with milk, or milk rice with lunu miris.
Lunch: half the plate vegetables, a quarter rice, a quarter protein.
Snacks: a banana, peanuts, curd or a boiled egg instead of biscuits.
Keep a water bottle on your desk.
Avoid very heavy meals right before an exam.

body.key_point: Regular meals with protein and whole grains keep your energy and focus steady through exam days.

myths.myth: An energy drink is a good breakfast before an exam.
myths.fact: Caffeine and sugar give a short boost, then a crash. A real breakfast lasts longer.

body.takeaway: Never sit an exam on an empty stomach. Even a quick banana and milk is better than nothing.
body.try_this: Plan tomorrow's breakfast tonight and keep it ready, even if it's just bread, an egg and a banana.
body.seek_help: If stress has taken away your appetite for weeks, or you're losing weight, talk to a doctor or counsellor.

references.label: Adolphus K, Lawton CL, Champ CL, Dye L. The effects of breakfast and breakfast composition on cognition in children and adolescents: a systematic review. Advances in Nutrition. 2016;7(3):590S-612S.
Nutrition Division, Ministry of Health Sri Lanka. Food Based Dietary Guidelines for Sri Lankans. 2021.

title: Heart Health Starts at University
subtitle: Why young adults should care about blood pressure and cholesterol

body.hook: Heart attacks are for older people, right? The habits that lead to them start much earlier, often right here at university.

sections.heading: The situation in Sri Lanka
sections.text: Heart disease, stroke and diabetes are among the leading causes of death in Sri Lanka. In the national STEPS survey in 2021, about one in three adults had raised blood pressure and around four in ten were overweight. A study of University of Peradeniya students found that some already had high triglycerides and raised blood pressure.

sections.heading: What raises your risk
sections.text: Most risk factors are habits you can change.
bullets: Too much salt, fried food and sugary drinks
Too few vegetables and fruits
Sitting most of the day and little exercise
Smoking and heavy drinking
Long-term stress and poor sleep
Carrying extra weight around the waist

sections.heading: Know your numbers
sections.text: High blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol usually have no symptoms. The only way to know is to measure them. Get your blood pressure checked at least once a year, and a fasting blood sugar and lipid test if a doctor advises it.

body.key_point: Most heart disease is preventable. What you eat, how much you move and whether you smoke matter more than your age.

myths.myth: I'm young and fit, so my blood pressure must be fine.
myths.fact: High blood pressure can affect young adults and has no symptoms. Only measuring tells you.

body.takeaway: Know your blood pressure, waist and blood sugar, and build heart-healthy habits now.
body.try_this: Get your blood pressure measured at the health centre this month and log it in VitalU.
body.seek_help: Get urgent help (call 1990) for chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, sudden breathlessness, or weakness on one side of the body.

references.label: World Health Organization. Cardiovascular diseases (fact sheet).
Ministry of Health Sri Lanka and WHO. Sri Lanka STEPS NCD Risk Factor Survey 2021.
Ralapanawa DMPUK et al. Prevalence of metabolic syndrome and its components among university students at the University of Peradeniya. iPURSE 2023 Proceedings.

title: Racing Heart Before Exams? What Your Body Is Telling You
subtitle: Why your pulse climbs and how to calm it

body.hook: Walking into the exam hall and feeling your heart pound in your chest? That's your stress response doing exactly what it was designed to do.

sections.heading: What happens in your body
sections.text: When you feel under pressure, your body releases adrenaline and cortisol. Your heart beats faster, you breathe more quickly and your muscles tense, ready for action. A normal resting heart rate for adults is about 60 to 100 beats a minute; it can jump well above that during stress and settle again afterwards.

sections.heading: When stress becomes a problem
sections.text: Short bursts of stress are normal and can even sharpen focus. But stress that never switches off, with poor sleep, too much caffeine and no breaks, keeps blood pressure and heart rate up and wears you down.

sections.heading: Calm your heart in minutes
sections.text: These are quick to do anywhere.
bullets: Slow breathing: breathe out longer than you breathe in for 1 to 2 minutes.
Relax your shoulders and unclench your jaw.
Limit coffee, energy drinks and strong tea before exams.
Move: a 10-minute walk burns off stress hormones.
Sleep well the night before instead of an all-nighter.

body.key_point: A racing heart under stress is normal. Slow breathing and good sleep help it settle quickly.

myths.myth: A fast heartbeat before an exam means something is wrong with your heart.
myths.fact: It's usually a normal stress response that settles once you relax.

body.takeaway: Your stress response is on your side. Learn to switch it off as well as on.
body.try_this: Before your next exam, sit quietly and breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6 counts, ten times.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if your heart races or flutters when you are resting, or with chest pain, fainting or breathlessness.

references.label: American Heart Association. All about heart rate (pulse).
Zaccaro A et al. How breath-control can change your life: a systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. 2018;12:353.

title: What Smoking Really Does to Your Lungs
subtitle: See the damage, and how quickly your body starts to heal

body.hook: 'Just one with friends after exams' can quietly turn into a pack a week. What is all that smoke doing inside you?

sections.heading: Inside the lungs
sections.text: Your airways are lined with tiny hairs called cilia that sweep out dust and germs. Cigarette smoke paralyses and destroys them, so mucus and tar build up. Over time, the tiny air sacs (alveoli) where oxygen enters your blood are damaged and can't be repaired. That is how smoking leads to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and lung cancer.

sections.heading: More than the lungs
sections.text: Tobacco harms almost every organ. It narrows blood vessels and raises the risk of heart attack and stroke, causes gum disease and stained teeth, ages the skin and lowers fitness. Tobacco kills more than 8 million people worldwide every year.

sections.heading: E-cigarettes and vapes
sections.text: Vapes still deliver nicotine, which is highly addictive, and many contain other harmful chemicals. They are not a safe alternative for young people.

sections.heading: Your body starts healing fast
sections.text: Within hours of stopping, carbon monoxide levels in your blood drop. Within weeks to months, circulation and breathing improve and coughing eases. After a year, the extra risk of heart disease falls by about half.

body.key_point: Every cigarette damages your lungs and heart, and every day without smoking helps them recover.

myths.myth: Social smoking now and then is harmless.
myths.fact: There is no safe level of smoking. Even light smoking raises heart disease risk.

myths.myth: Beedi is less harmful than cigarettes.
myths.fact: Beedis deliver as much or more nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide.

body.takeaway: It's never too early or too late to stop. The benefits start within hours.
body.try_this: If you smoke, pick a quit date this month, tell a friend, and remove cigarettes and lighters from your room.
body.seek_help: Free help to quit is available from the National Authority on Tobacco and Alcohol (NATA) helpline 1948, and from the University Health Centre (081 239 2022).

tools.label: Talk to a doctor about quitting

references.label: World Health Organization. Tobacco (fact sheet).
NHS. Quit smoking.
World Health Organization. Tobacco: e-cigarettes (questions and answers).

title: Alcohol and Your Body: The Honest Facts
subtitle: What happens after 'just a few drinks'

body.hook: Batch party this weekend and everyone's drinking? Here's what that alcohol actually does, so you can make your own informed choice.

sections.heading: What alcohol does
sections.text: Alcohol slows down the brain, which affects judgement, coordination and memory. It irritates the stomach, adds empty calories and disturbs sleep, even if it helps you fall asleep at first. Heavy drinking damages the liver, raises blood pressure and is linked to several cancers.

sections.heading: No safe level
sections.text: The World Health Organization says there is no amount of alcohol that is completely safe for health. The less you drink, the lower the risk.

sections.heading: If you choose to drink
sections.text: Reduce the harm.
bullets: Eat a proper meal first and drink water between drinks.
Set a limit before you start and stick to it.
Never drink and drive or ride with someone who has been drinking.
Look out for friends and don't leave anyone alone when drunk.
Don't mix alcohol with medicines or other drugs.

body.key_point: Less alcohol is always better for your health. It's completely fine to say no.

myths.myth: Alcohol helps you sleep better.
myths.fact: It may help you fall asleep, but it breaks up deep sleep later in the night.

body.takeaway: You don't need alcohol to have fun or fit in. Choosing not to drink is a strong choice.
body.try_this: Plan an alcohol-free way to celebrate after exams, like a trip, a match or a meal with friends.
body.seek_help: If you feel you need alcohol to cope, or can't cut down, call the NATA helpline 1948 or talk to a counsellor. In an emergency (unconscious, vomiting while drowsy, slow breathing) call 1990.

references.label: World Health Organization. Alcohol (fact sheet).
Anderson BO et al. Health and cancer risks associated with low levels of alcohol consumption. The Lancet Public Health. 2023;8(1):e6-e7.

title: Always Tired? It Could Be Anaemia
subtitle: Signs of low iron and how to eat your way back

body.hook: Tired even after a full night's sleep, breathless on the stairs to your lecture hall, and pale? Before blaming exams, think about your iron.

sections.heading: What anaemia is
sections.text: Anaemia means your blood has less haemoglobin than it should, so less oxygen reaches your body. The most common cause is not having enough iron. It is very common in young women in Sri Lanka because of monthly blood loss and low iron intake.

sections.heading: Signs to look for
sections.text: Signs build up slowly, so they're easy to miss.
bullets: Tiredness and lack of energy
Shortness of breath and a fast heartbeat
Pale skin, inside of eyelids or nails
Headaches, dizziness and poor concentration
Brittle nails, hair fall, cravings for ice or clay

sections.heading: Eat for iron
sections.text: Combine iron foods with vitamin C to absorb more.
bullets: Iron from animal foods is best absorbed: fish, sprats, chicken, eggs, liver.
Plant sources: dhal, chickpeas, green gram, gotukola, mukunuwenna, kankun.
Add vitamin C: lime on your mallung, a guava or orange after meals.
Avoid tea and coffee with meals. Have them at least an hour apart.

body.key_point: Iron-rich food plus a source of vitamin C at the same meal is the simplest way to protect against anaemia.

myths.myth: If I feel tired, I should just start iron tablets.
myths.fact: Get a blood test first. Tiredness has many causes, and too much iron can be harmful.

body.takeaway: Persistent tiredness deserves a simple blood test (a full blood count, FBC).
body.try_this: Squeeze lime on your gotukola mallung and have tea an hour after lunch instead of with it, all this week.
body.seek_help: See a doctor for a full blood count if you have several of the signs above, very heavy periods, or feel breathless at rest.

references.label: World Health Organization. Anaemia (fact sheet).
NHS. Iron deficiency anaemia.

title: Headaches and Migraine During Semester
subtitle: Common triggers, quick relief and when to worry

body.hook: Throbbing headache after a long day of slides and screens? You're far from alone. Headaches are one of the most common health complaints worldwide.

sections.heading: Tension headache or migraine?
sections.text: Tension headaches feel like a tight band around the head and are often linked to stress, poor posture and tiredness. Migraine is a throbbing headache, often on one side, that can come with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, and can last hours to days.

sections.heading: Common triggers for students
sections.text: Triggers vary from person to person.
bullets: Not drinking enough water
Skipping meals
Too little or irregular sleep
Long screen time and bright light
Stress, and too much or suddenly stopping caffeine
For some, hormone changes around periods

sections.heading: What helps
sections.text: Rest in a quiet, dim room, drink water, eat something and use a cold or warm compress. Simple pain relievers can help if taken early, but using them on more than 10 days a month can cause more headaches.

body.key_point: Regular meals, water and sleep prevent many headaches. A headache diary helps you spot your triggers.

myths.myth: Taking painkillers every day is fine for frequent headaches.
myths.fact: Overuse can cause 'medication-overuse headache'. See a doctor instead.

body.takeaway: Notice what happened before each headache. Patterns point to triggers you can avoid.
body.try_this: For two weeks, note each headache with your sleep, meals and water that day.
body.seek_help: Get urgent help for a sudden, severe 'worst ever' headache, headache with fever and stiff neck, confusion, weakness, or after a head injury. See a doctor if headaches are frequent.

references.label: World Health Organization. Headache disorders (fact sheet).
NHS. Migraine.

title: Burning Stomach? Gastritis and Acid Reflux
subtitle: Protecting your stomach on a busy student schedule

body.hook: That burning feeling under your ribs after skipping lunch and having plain tea instead? Your stomach is asking for a break.

sections.heading: What's going on
sections.text: Gastritis means the stomach lining is irritated or inflamed. Acid reflux is when stomach acid moves up into the food pipe, causing heartburn. Both cause burning pain, bloating, nausea and feeling full quickly.

sections.heading: Common causes
sections.text: Several things can irritate the stomach.
bullets: Long gaps between meals and skipped breakfast
Very spicy, oily or fried food
Painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin, especially on an empty stomach
Smoking and alcohol
Stress
An infection called Helicobacter pylori

sections.heading: Eat gently
sections.text: Small changes calm most symptoms.
bullets: Eat smaller meals at regular times.
Have a mild breakfast like kanji, bread, oats or a banana.
Go easy on chilli, deep-fried food and very sour pickles.
Don't lie down for 2 to 3 hours after eating.
Avoid painkillers on an empty stomach.

body.key_point: Regular, smaller meals and fewer irritants calm most stomach burning.

myths.myth: Milk is the best cure for gastritis.
myths.fact: Milk may soothe briefly, but it can trigger more acid later.

body.takeaway: Your stomach likes routine. Don't leave it empty for long.
body.try_this: Eat something small every 3 to 4 hours this week and note whether the burning improves.
body.seek_help: See a doctor urgently if you vomit blood or something like coffee grounds, have black stools, severe pain, or difficulty swallowing. See a doctor if symptoms last more than two weeks.

references.label: NHS. Indigestion.
NHS. Heartburn and acid reflux.

title: Breakouts Before Presentations? Understanding Acne
subtitle: What really causes pimples and what helps

body.hook: Why does a pimple always appear the day before a big presentation? Stress, hormones and habits all play a part.

sections.heading: What causes acne
sections.text: Acne starts when hair follicles get blocked with oil and dead skin. Bacteria and inflammation then cause spots. Hormone changes, genes, stress and some medicines all affect how much oil your skin makes. Acne is very common in young adults and is not caused by being dirty.

sections.heading: Everyday skin care
sections.text: Simple and gentle works best.
bullets: Wash your face twice a day with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water.
Don't scrub hard or use harsh products; they irritate the skin.
Use oil-free, non-comedogenic moisturisers and sunscreen.
Don't squeeze or pick spots, which can leave scars.
Change your pillowcase often and keep your phone screen clean.

sections.heading: Food and acne
sections.text: Evidence suggests that high-sugar foods and lots of refined carbohydrates may worsen acne in some people. A balanced diet with vegetables, fruit and whole grains is good for your skin and the rest of you.

body.key_point: Gentle care, patience and not picking help most acne. Treatments take 6 to 8 weeks to work.

myths.myth: Toothpaste dries out pimples.
myths.fact: It can irritate and burn the skin. Use proper acne products instead.

body.takeaway: Be gentle with your skin, and give any new routine at least two months.
body.try_this: For the next month, wash your face twice a day with a mild cleanser and stop touching or picking spots.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if acne is painful, leaves scars or dark marks, or is affecting your confidence. Prescription treatments work well.

references.label: NHS. Acne.
American Academy of Dermatology. Acne: tips for managing.

title: Fresh All Day: Sweat, Body Odour and Oral Care
subtitle: Simple hygiene habits for hot, busy campus days

body.hook: Kandy's heat, a crowded bus and back-to-back lectures. How do you stay fresh until evening?

sections.heading: Why we smell
sections.text: Sweat itself has almost no smell. Body odour happens when bacteria on the skin break sweat down, especially in the armpits and feet. It's normal, and good habits keep it under control.

sections.heading: Stay fresh
sections.text: A few daily habits make a big difference.
bullets: Shower once a day, and after sport, using soap on armpits, groin and feet.
Dry yourself well, especially between the toes.
Use an antiperspirant or deodorant on clean, dry skin.
Wear clean, loose cotton clothes and change socks daily.
Wash and dry clothes fully in the sun.

sections.heading: Fresh breath and healthy teeth
sections.text: Brush twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, clean between your teeth, and clean your tongue. Cut down on sugary drinks and snacks, and drink water. See a dentist once a year.

body.key_point: Daily washing, dry clean clothes and twice-daily brushing keep you fresh and confident.

myths.myth: Antiperspirants are dangerous.
myths.fact: There's no good evidence that they cause cancer or other serious disease.

body.takeaway: Hygiene is simple, daily and part of feeling confident around others.
body.try_this: Keep a small kit in your bag: deodorant, a spare pair of socks, and a travel toothbrush.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if sweating is very heavy and affects daily life, if odour changes suddenly, or if you have bleeding gums or toothache.

references.label: NHS. Body odour (BO).
World Health Organization. Oral health (fact sheet).

title: The 4-7-8 Breath: A One-Minute Calm-Down Tool
subtitle: Slow breathing for exam panic and racing thoughts

body.hook: Your mind goes blank in the exam hall, your heart races and your hands are cold. One minute of slow breathing can turn that around.

sections.heading: Why slow breathing works
sections.text: Breathing slowly, with a longer breath out, activates the body's 'rest and digest' system. Research shows that slow breathing lowers heart rate and helps people feel calmer and more in control.

sections.heading: How to do 4-7-8
sections.text: Sit comfortably and relax your shoulders.
bullets: Breathe in quietly through your nose for 4 counts.
Hold your breath gently for 7 counts.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 8 counts.
Repeat 4 times. If holding feels uncomfortable, shorten the counts but keep the out-breath longest.

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.text: Before an exam or presentation, when you can't sleep, or whenever worry spins out of control. It works better the more you practise, so try it daily when you're calm.

body.key_point: A breath out that is longer than the breath in tells your body it is safe to calm down.

myths.myth: Breathing exercises only work for some people.
myths.fact: Most people feel calmer within a minute; regular practice makes the effect stronger.

body.takeaway: Your breath is a calming tool you always carry with you.
body.try_this: Practise 4-7-8 breathing for one minute before sleep every night this week.
body.seek_help: If anxiety or panic happens often, or stops you attending lectures, a counsellor can help. In a crisis, call 1926.

references.label: Zaccaro A et al. How breath-control can change your life: a systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. 2018;12:353.
NHS. Breathing exercises for stress.

title: Brain Breaks: Why Stepping Away From Screens Helps You Focus
subtitle: How short breaks restore attention during long study sessions

body.hook: Three hours on the same chapter and you've read the same paragraph five times? Your attention needs a reset, not more effort.

sections.heading: Why focus fades
sections.text: Attention naturally drops when you do one task for a long time. Research shows that brief breaks, even a few minutes long, help people stay focused on long tasks. Endless scrolling during 'breaks' doesn't give your brain the same rest.

sections.heading: Make breaks count
sections.text: A good break moves your body and rests your eyes.
bullets: Study in blocks of 25 to 50 minutes, then take a 5 to 15 minute break.
Stand up, stretch or walk to fill your water bottle.
Look out of a window at something far away.
Leave your phone face down during study blocks.
Talk to a friend or step outside for daylight.

sections.heading: Screens and sleep
sections.text: Late-night scrolling delays sleep and makes the next day's focus worse. Try to put screens away 30 minutes before bed.

body.key_point: Short, screen-free breaks help you focus longer, not shorter.

myths.myth: A 'dopamine detox' resets your brain chemistry.
myths.fact: That idea is overstated, but cutting distractions and taking real breaks does help focus.

body.takeaway: Plan your breaks like you plan your study.
body.try_this: Try four 45-minute study blocks today, each followed by a 10-minute walk or stretch without your phone.
body.seek_help: If you can't concentrate for weeks, along with low mood or poor sleep, talk to a counsellor or doctor.

references.label: Ariga A, Lleras A. Brief and rare mental 'breaks' keep you focused: deactivation and reactivation of task goals preempt vigilance decrements. Cognition. 2011;118(3):439-443.
World Health Organization. WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. 2020.

title: Pulled an All-Nighter? How to Reset Your Body Clock
subtitle: Getting your sleep back on track after exams

body.hook: Stayed up all night to finish an assignment and now you can't sleep at night or stay awake in the day? Your body clock is confused.

sections.heading: Your body clock
sections.text: Your circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour clock that tells you when to feel sleepy and alert. Light, especially morning daylight, is the strongest signal that sets it. Late nights, bright screens and irregular sleep times push it out of sync.

sections.heading: Why all-nighters backfire
sections.text: Sleep is when your brain stores what you've learned. Missing it hurts memory, focus and mood the next day, and can lower your exam performance. Adults need 7 to 9 hours a night.

sections.heading: How to reset
sections.text: Be consistent for a few days.
bullets: Wake up at the same time every day, even after a bad night.
Get outside into daylight for 15 minutes in the morning.
Avoid naps longer than 20 to 30 minutes, and none after 3 PM.
No caffeine after early afternoon.
Dim lights and screens an hour before bed.

body.key_point: A fixed wake-up time and morning light reset your body clock fastest.

myths.myth: You can fully catch up on lost sleep at the weekend.
myths.fact: Sleeping in helps a little, but regular sleep every night is what restores focus and mood.

body.takeaway: Protect your sleep during exams; it is part of studying.
body.try_this: Set the same wake-up alarm for the next seven days and step outside within an hour of waking.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if you can't sleep most nights for more than three weeks, or feel very sleepy during the day despite enough sleep.

references.label: Hirshkowitz M et al. National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations. Sleep Health. 2015;1(1):40-43.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About sleep.

title: Tired All the Time? Better Sleep in a Busy Hostel
subtitle: Sleep habits that work even with noisy roommates

body.hook: Lights on, roommates chatting, phone buzzing at 1 AM. Good sleep in a hostel can feel impossible, but small changes really help.

sections.heading: Why sleep matters
sections.text: Good sleep strengthens memory, mood, immunity and appetite control. Short sleep is linked to weight gain, poor concentration and a higher risk of illness over time.

sections.heading: Build a sleep routine
sections.text: Habits that help most people sleep better are called sleep hygiene.
bullets: Go to bed and wake up at similar times every day.
Keep your bed for sleeping, not studying or scrolling.
Use earplugs and an eye mask in a shared room.
Avoid caffeine after early afternoon and heavy meals late at night.
Wind down with a shower, light reading or slow breathing.
If you can't sleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something calm until sleepy.

sections.heading: Fighting daytime tiredness
sections.text: Get morning daylight, move during the day, drink water and eat regular meals. A short 20-minute nap can help, but long naps make night sleep harder.

body.key_point: Consistency beats perfection. Regular sleep and wake times improve how rested you feel.

myths.myth: Scrolling on your phone helps you relax before sleep.
myths.fact: Bright screens and stimulating content keep your brain alert and delay sleep.

body.takeaway: Treat your sleep like an important lecture you never skip.
body.try_this: Agree a 'lights low' time with your roommates this week and use earplugs if needed.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if you snore loudly and stop breathing in your sleep, or if tiredness lasts weeks despite good sleep habits.

references.label: NHS. How to get to sleep.
Hirshkowitz M et al. National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations. Sleep Health. 2015;1(1):40-43.

title: Nervous About Interviews? Build Real Confidence
subtitle: Calm nerves and show your best self

body.hook: Your first internship interview is next week and your stomach is already in knots. The good news: confidence can be prepared.

sections.heading: Nerves are normal
sections.text: Feeling nervous shows that the interview matters to you. A little stress can even sharpen your focus. The aim is not to feel no nerves, but to stay calm enough to think clearly.

sections.heading: Prepare well
sections.text: Preparation is the biggest confidence booster.
bullets: Research the organisation and the role.
Prepare short examples of times you solved a problem, worked in a team or learned from a mistake.
Practise answers out loud with a friend.
Plan your clothes and route the day before.
Prepare two questions to ask them.

sections.heading: On the day
sections.text: Eat a proper meal, arrive early and use slow breathing while you wait. Sit upright, make friendly eye contact, and take a moment to think before answering. It's fine to say 'Let me think about that.'

body.key_point: Preparation and slow breathing do more for confidence than any trick.

myths.myth: Holding a 'power pose' for two minutes changes your hormones and guarantees confidence.
myths.fact: Larger studies did not confirm the hormone effect. Preparation and practice help far more.

body.takeaway: Confidence comes from preparation, not from never feeling nervous.
body.try_this: Write down three short stories about your strengths and practise telling each in under a minute.
body.seek_help: If anxiety stops you attending interviews or presentations, a counsellor can teach you techniques that work.

references.label: Ranehill E et al. Assessing the robustness of power posing: no effect on hormones and risk tolerance in a large sample of men and women. Psychological Science. 2015;26(5):653-656.
Zaccaro A et al. How breath-control can change your life. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. 2018;12:353.

title: Speak So People Listen: Communication and Body Language
subtitle: Presence that doesn't depend on how you look

body.hook: Ever felt invisible in a group discussion, even when you had a good idea? How you speak and carry yourself can help your ideas be heard.

sections.heading: Presence is a skill
sections.text: Presence is not about looks or expensive clothes. It's about being clear, calm and genuinely interested in others. Like any skill, it improves with practice.

sections.heading: Simple habits that help
sections.text: Small changes make a big difference.
bullets: Stand or sit tall with your shoulders relaxed. Good posture also helps you breathe and speak clearly.
Make friendly eye contact, but you don't need to stare.
Speak a little slower than feels natural, and pause between points.
Listen fully before replying, and refer to what others said.
Use your hands naturally to explain ideas.

sections.heading: Look after yourself
sections.text: Clean, neat clothes that fit, good hygiene and enough sleep help you feel ready. Confidence also grows when you look after your health.

body.key_point: Clear speaking, good listening and relaxed posture build presence for everyone, whatever they look like.

myths.myth: Confident people never feel nervous.
myths.fact: Most confident speakers feel nervous; they've just practised managing it.

body.takeaway: Slow down, listen well, and let your posture support your voice.
body.try_this: In your next group discussion, wait for a pause, take a breath, and share one idea slowly and clearly.
body.seek_help: If shyness or social anxiety holds you back a lot, a counsellor can help you build confidence step by step.

references.label: NHS. Social anxiety (social phobia).

title: Hydration Hacks: Why You Feel Tired at 2 PM in Lecture
subtitle: Beat the afternoon slump with a water bottle

body.hook: Heavy eyes in your 2 PM lecture? Before blaming the lecturer, check your water bottle.

sections.heading: Why water matters
sections.text: Even mild dehydration, losing just 1 to 2% of your body water, can make you tired, give you a headache and hurt your concentration. In Sri Lanka's heat, with walking between faculties, you lose water faster than you think.

sections.heading: How much you need
sections.text: Most young adults need about 2 to 2.5 litres of fluids a day, more in hot weather or when active. Your urine colour is a simple guide: pale yellow means you're well hydrated.

sections.heading: Easy habits
sections.text: Make water the easy choice.
bullets: Carry a refillable bottle and refill it at lunch.
Drink a glass of water with every meal.
Have water before you feel thirsty, especially in the afternoon.
Choose water or king coconut over sugary drinks.
Fruits like watermelon and oranges add water too.

body.key_point: Small, regular sips through the day keep your energy and focus steady.

myths.myth: You must drink exactly 8 glasses a day.
myths.fact: Needs vary with your size, activity and the weather. Use thirst and urine colour as guides.

body.takeaway: Keep your bottle visible and sip often.
body.try_this: Finish one bottle of water before lunch and one before 5 PM every day this week.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if you are always very thirsty, pass large amounts of urine, or feel dizzy and faint.

references.label: Popkin BM, D'Anci KE, Rosenberg IH. Water, hydration, and health. Nutrition Reviews. 2010;68(8):439-458.
Adan A. Cognitive performance and dehydration. Journal of the American College of Nutrition. 2012;31(2):71-78.
EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies. Scientific opinion on dietary reference values for water. EFSA Journal. 2010;8(3):1459.

title: Electrolyte Drinks or Plain Water?
subtitle: What your body really needs during long library days and sport

body.hook: Sports drinks look healthy and the adverts say you need them. Do you, really?

sections.heading: What electrolytes are
sections.text: Electrolytes like sodium and potassium help your muscles and nerves work and keep your body's water in balance. You lose some in sweat.

sections.heading: When plain water is enough
sections.text: For studying, normal walking and exercise under about an hour, water and regular meals give you everything you need. Most sports drinks also contain a lot of sugar.

sections.heading: When you may need more
sections.text: Electrolytes help in some situations.
bullets: Long, intense sport over about an hour, especially in heat
Heavy sweating in very hot weather
Diarrhoea or vomiting: use oral rehydration salts (Jeevani)
King coconut water is a natural, lower-sugar option after sport

body.key_point: For everyday student life, water is all you need. Save electrolyte drinks for long sport or illness.

myths.myth: Sports drinks are healthier than soft drinks.
myths.fact: Many contain similar amounts of sugar.

body.takeaway: Water first; oral rehydration salts when you're sick; sports drinks rarely.
body.try_this: Next time you reach for a sports drink while studying, swap it for water or king coconut.
body.seek_help: Get medical help if you have severe vomiting or diarrhoea, can't keep fluids down, or feel confused or very weak.

references.label: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN et al. Exercise and fluid replacement (position stand). Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2007;39(2):377-390.
World Health Organization. Diarrhoeal disease (fact sheet).

title: Beating Constipation With Fibre and Fluids
subtitle: Simple, gut-friendly habits for hostel life

body.hook: New hostel, new food, odd routine, and now your stomach won't cooperate? Constipation is very common when your routine changes.

sections.heading: What constipation is
sections.text: Constipation means passing stools less than three times a week, or stools that are hard, dry and difficult to pass. Low fibre, too little water, little activity and ignoring the urge to go are common causes.

sections.heading: Fibre-rich Sri Lankan foods
sections.text: Adults need about 25 grams of fibre a day. These help.
bullets: Red rice, kurakkan and atta roti instead of white flour foods
Dhal, chickpeas and green gram
Vegetables and leafy mallung at every main meal
Fruits like papaya, guava, banana and wood apple
Add fibre slowly, with extra water, to avoid bloating

sections.heading: Other habits that help
sections.text: Drink plenty of water, stay active, and don't ignore the urge to go. Try to give yourself time in the morning after breakfast, when the bowel is most active.

body.key_point: More fibre, more water and more movement solve most constipation.

myths.myth: Daily laxatives are a good long-term fix.
myths.fact: Regular laxative use should be guided by a doctor. Food and fluids come first.

body.takeaway: Your gut loves fibre, water and routine.
body.try_this: Add one fruit and one extra serving of vegetables every day this week, plus an extra glass of water.
body.seek_help: See a doctor if constipation lasts more than three weeks, or comes with blood in the stool, weight loss, severe pain or a big change in bowel habits.

references.label: NHS. Constipation.
World Health Organization. Healthy diet (fact sheet).

title: Eating Well on a Student Budget
subtitle: Balanced Sri Lankan meals that don't cost a lot

body.hook: Only a few hundred rupees left until the end of the month? You can still eat well. Some of the healthiest Sri Lankan foods are also the cheapest.

sections.heading: Build a balanced plate
sections.text: Fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with rice or another starch, and a quarter with protein. This works for a canteen rice and curry, a home meal or a cheap boarding meal.

sections.heading: Cheap and nutritious choices
sections.text: Get the most nutrition for your money.
bullets: Dhal, chickpeas, green gram and soya: cheap, filling protein
Eggs and sprats (halmasso): affordable animal protein and calcium
Seasonal vegetables and leafy greens like gotukola and kankun
Bananas, papaya and guava instead of packaged snacks
Red rice or kurakkan: more fibre for a similar price

sections.heading: Save money and eat better
sections.text: Short eats and soft drinks add up fast. Sharing cooking with friends, buying vegetables in season and carrying water instead of buying drinks can save money every week.

body.key_point: Pulses, eggs, sprats, seasonal vegetables and local fruit give great nutrition for little money.

myths.myth: Healthy food is always expensive.
myths.fact: Many Sri Lankan staples like dhal, gotukola and bananas are both cheap and nutritious.

body.takeaway: Plan simple meals around pulses, vegetables and local fruit.
body.try_this: Use the Budget Planner to plan next week's meals within your budget.
body.seek_help: If money worries mean you often skip meals, the university welfare services or a counsellor may be able to help.

references.label: Nutrition Division, Ministry of Health Sri Lanka. Food Based Dietary Guidelines for Sri Lankans. 2021.
World Health Organization. Healthy diet (fact sheet).

title: Small Habits, Big Changes
subtitle: How to build healthy habits that actually stick

body.hook: Started a new health plan with great energy, then gave up after a week? It's not you. It's how habits work.

sections.heading: How habits form
sections.text: A habit forms when you repeat an action in the same situation until it becomes automatic. In one study, it took on average about 66 days, with a wide range from 18 to over 200 days. Missing one day didn't stop the habit forming.

sections.heading: Make habits easy
sections.text: Small and specific beats big and vague.
bullets: Start tiny: one glass of water after waking, not 'drink more water'.
Link it to something you already do: stretch after brushing your teeth.
Make it easy: keep fruit on your desk and your water bottle in your bag.
Track it. Seeing a streak keeps you going.
If you miss a day, just start again tomorrow.

sections.heading: Your habits in VitalU
sections.text: VitalU looks at your logs for water, steps, sleep and meals and suggests the habits that will help you most. Start with the one that feels easiest.

body.key_point: Tiny, repeated actions in the same situation become habits. Consistency matters more than perfection.

myths.myth: It takes exactly 21 days to form a habit.
myths.fact: It varies a lot, often around two months. Keep going.

body.takeaway: Pick one tiny habit and attach it to something you already do every day.
body.try_this: Choose one habit from your Home screen and do it every day for the next two weeks.
body.seek_help: If you feel stuck or unmotivated for weeks, talking to a counsellor can help you find a way forward.

references.label: Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J. How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology. 2010;40(6):998-1009.

title: STIs: What Every Student Should Know
subtitle: Common infections, signs and how to protect yourself

body.hook: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are common, often silent and easy to prevent. Knowing the facts protects you and the people you care about.

sections.heading: What STIs are
sections.text: STIs are infections passed through vaginal, anal or oral sex, and sometimes through skin contact. Common ones include chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes, HPV and HIV. More than 1 million STIs are acquired every day worldwide.

sections.heading: Many have no symptoms
sections.text: Many people with an STI feel completely well, so they can pass it on without knowing. When there are signs, they can include:
bullets: Unusual discharge from the penis or vagina
Pain or burning when passing urine
Sores, blisters, lumps or warts around the genitals or mouth
Itching, rashes, or pain during sex
Bleeding between periods or after sex

sections.heading: How to protect yourself
sections.text: Prevention is simple and effective.
bullets: Use a condom correctly every time you have sex.
Get tested if you've had unprotected sex or a new partner.
Get the HPV vaccine if you haven't had it.
Talk openly with partners about testing.
Alcohol and drugs make risky choices more likely.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Untreated STIs can cause pelvic pain, infertility, problems in pregnancy, and raise the risk of HIV. Most STIs are curable, and all can be treated, especially when found early.

body.key_point: Condoms and regular testing prevent most STIs. Many infections have no symptoms, so testing is the only way to know.

myths.myth: You can tell if someone has an STI by looking at them.
myths.fact: Most people with an STI have no visible signs.

myths.myth: You can't get an STI from oral sex.
myths.fact: Several STIs, including herpes, gonorrhoea and syphilis, can spread through oral sex.

body.takeaway: Protect yourself every time, and get tested without fear. It's routine healthcare.
body.try_this: Save the Kandy STD clinic number (081 220 3622) in your phone so you have it if you ever need it.
body.seek_help: If you notice any of the signs above, or had sex without a condom, visit an STD clinic. Testing and treatment at government STD clinics are free and confidential.

referral.text: Free, confidential testing, treatment and advice from the government STD clinic in Kandy (National STD/AIDS Control Programme). No one else is told about your visit.
referral.label: Call 081 220 3622

title: Getting Tested: Free, Confidential and Simple
subtitle: What happens at an STD clinic in Sri Lanka

body.hook: Worried about a possible infection but scared someone will find out? Here's exactly what happens when you visit an STD clinic, and why there's no need to fear it.

sections.heading: Where to go
sections.text: Sri Lanka has government STD clinics in every district, run by the National STD/AIDS Control Programme. The clinic in Kandy is closest to campus. Services, including HIV testing, are free of charge.

sections.heading: Confidential and non-judgemental
sections.text: Staff are trained to treat everyone with respect and privacy, whatever your age, gender or sexuality. Your results are not shared with your family, university or anyone else without your permission.

sections.heading: What happens at a visit
sections.text: A typical visit is simple.
bullets: You talk privately with a doctor about any symptoms and your risks.
You may have a short examination.
Tests are usually a blood test, a urine sample or a swab.
Many results are ready within a few days.
If you have an infection, treatment is provided and partners can be offered testing too.

sections.heading: When to get tested
sections.text: Get tested if you have symptoms, after unprotected sex or a condom breaking, when you start a new relationship, or if a partner has an STI. After a possible HIV exposure, go within 72 hours, as preventive medicine (PEP) may be available.

body.key_point: STI testing at government clinics in Sri Lanka is free, confidential and quick. Early testing means easy treatment.

myths.myth: Only people with many partners need testing.
myths.fact: Anyone who is sexually active can get an STI. Testing is routine healthcare.

body.takeaway: Testing is a responsible, normal part of looking after your health.
body.try_this: If you are sexually active, plan a routine check-up at the STD clinic, even if you feel fine.
body.seek_help: Visit the STD clinic straight away if you have symptoms or a possible exposure. For possible HIV exposure, go within 72 hours.

referral.title: Medical Officer, STD Clinic, Kandy
referral.text: Talk to the medical officer at the STD clinic in Kandy for confidential advice, testing and treatment. Services are free.
referral.label: Call 081 220 3622

references.label: National STD/AIDS Control Programme, Ministry of Health Sri Lanka. Contact details of STD clinics, 2023.
Family Planning Association of Sri Lanka. Checking in on your sexual health.
World Health Organization. HIV and AIDS (fact sheet).
